## Objectives    {#sec-objectives}

In this lab, we describe original features fo language `R`. 
Language `R` is not regarded as an Object Oriented (OO) language in the same way 
as `C++`, 'Java', or `Python`. Indeed, the lineage of `R` goes back to [`Scheme`](https://www.scheme.org), a functional language. 

Nevertheless, `R` offers users and developers several Object Oriented frameworks. In @sec-s3,  we showcase the oldest such framework named `S3`. In order to explore `S3`, we use base `R` and packages  `sloop`, `lobstr`, `generics`, and `rlang`. `S3` classes and generic functions play an important role in the `tidyverse` (`autoplot` within `ggplot2`, `augment`, `tidy` and `glance` in `broom`, to mention a few). 

In @sec-dplyr-ggplot-programming, we move to a practical and fundamental issue: programming with functions from `dplyr` and `ggplot2.` Functions from `dplyr` and `ggplot2` are tailored 
to interactive computations. Using *data masking*, they relieve us from quoting each and every column name, they allow us to write readable pipelines. When it comes to programming 
with `dplyr` verbs, things get more tricky: passing columns as arguments becomes more difficult because of  *data masking*. Nevertheless, the tidyverse offers simple devices to circumvent these impediments. 

*Data masking* is one facet of *tidy/lazy evaluation* that makes `R` so suitable for data exploration. `R`'s ability to handle expressions and environments as first-class objects is the most interesting aspect of the language. The ability to capture functions calls within the very body of functions is one benefit garnered this reflective power. In @sec-inside-lm, we showcase this possibility by inspecting the body of `lm`. 

In @sec-tidy-eval, we describe some applications of *tidy evaluation* as suggested by the eponymous cheatsheet.

## Generics and S3 classes  {#sec-s3}


Let us first create an instance of class `lm`. This object will serve as an instance 
of an S3 class. 
```{r}
#| label: build-lm-instance
lm0  <- lm(Gas ~ Insul * Temp, MASS::whiteside) # <1>
```
1. `lm` denotes both a function and the *class* of the result returned by the function. The function acts as a constructor for the class. 

::: {.callout-note title='Question'} 

- What does function `class()` do? 
- Is it possible to belong to type `list`  and to class `lm` simultaneously?
- In `R` what is an *attribute*? 
- How do we *set* and *get* attributes?  
- What does function `inherits()` do?
 
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile='solution'} 

::: {.callout-tip title='Solution'} 
 
```{r}
#| label: class-and-friends
#|
rlang::typeof(lm0) # <1>
is.list(lm0)       # <2>
attributes(lm0)    # <3>
inherits(lm0,"list")  
inherits(lm0, "lm")  # <4>
```
1. `lm0` is a list (with 13 named elements)
2. `lm0` is not just a list 
3. `lm0` has a `class` attribute
4. What an object inherits from depends on its `class` attribute. 



```{r}
#| label: attributes

attr(lm0, "class")
attr(lm0, "class") <- c("elephant", "animal")
attr(lm0, "class")        # <1> 
inherits(lm0, "animal")   # <2>
inherits(lm0, "elephant") # <3> 
typeof(lm0)
attr(lm0, "class") <- "lm"  # <4>
```
1. The `class` attribute is a vector of strings
2. An object may inherit from several classes
3. The components of the list `lm0` have not been affected
4. Everything is back in order 

::: 
 
:::

::: {.callout-note title='Question'} 

Load package `sloop`.

- What does `sloop::otype()` do? Apply it to an object of class `lm`.
- What happens when we first `unclass()` the object?
 
:::


::: {.content-visible when-profile='solution'} 
 
::: {.callout-tip title='Solution'} 
 

```{r}
#| label: 
sloop::otype(lm0)  # <1> 
sloop::otype(unclass(lm0))  # <2> 
attr(unclass(lm0), "class") # <3> 
all(lobstr::obj_addrs(lm0) == lobstr::obj_addrs(unclass(lm0))) # <4>
```
1. `otype()` 
2. Removing `class` attributes modifies `otype()` result
3. `unclass` removes the class attribute. 
4. The components of the list `lm0` have not been moved
::: 
:::

## Programming with `dplyr` and `ggplot2`  {#sec-dplyr-ggplot-programming}

We first aim at programming a function that takes as input a dataframe `df`, a column name `col`, and that, depending on the type of the column denoted by `col`, plots a histogram (for numerical column), a barplot (for factors), or raise an error of the column is neither categorical, nor numerical.

The function should return a ggplot object.

Here is a first attempt. 

Let us first build a toy tibble. 

```{r}
tb <- tibble( 
  col_num = rnorm(100), 
  col_fac = as_factor(sample(letters, 100, replace = T)), 
  col_ts = Sys.time() + duration(sample(1:20, 100, replace=T),units="days")
) 

tb |> 
  head()
```

::: {.content-visible when-profile='solution'} 
 
::: {.callout-tip title='Solution'} 
 

```{r}
gg_obj <-  function(df, col){
  
  vct <- df[[col]]  # <1>
  tp <- class(vct)

  if (tp != "numeric" & tp !="factor") {
    stop(paste0(col, " is of wrong type!"))
  }

  p <- ggplot(df) + 
    aes(x=.data[[col]])  # <2>

  if (tp=="numeric") {
    p <- p + geom_histogram()
  } else {
    p <- p + geom_bar()
  }

  p  
}

```
1. List component is accessed by name. `col` is a string. 
2. `.data` is a pronoun for the dataframe component of the `ggplot` object

```{r}
(
  gg_obj(tb, "col_num") +
    labs(
      title= "Histogram", 
      subtitle= "Numerical column")
) + (
  gg_obj(tb, "col_fac") +
    labs(
      title= "Barplot",
      subtitle= "Factor column"
    )
)
```

:::

:::


::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

- Avoid quoting the column name

:::

```{r}

  tp <- pull(df, col) # class(vct)

  if (tp != "numeric" & tp !="factor") {
    stop(paste0(col, " is of wrong type!"))
  }

  p <- ggplot(df) + 
    aes(x=col)  # <2>

  if (tp=="numeric") {
    p <- p + geom_histogram()
  } else {
    p <- p + geom_bar()
  }

  p  
}

```

::: {.content-visible when-profile='solution'} 
 
::: {.content-visible when-profile='solution'} 
 
```{r}
gg_obj_2 <-  function(df, col, ...){
  params <- list(...)
  vct <- pull(df, {{col}})
  tp <- class(vct)[1]

  if (tp != "numeric" & tp !="factor") {
    stop("column is of wrong type!")
    return
  }

  p <- ggplot(df) + 
    aes(x={{col}})  # <1>

  if (tp=="numeric") {
    p <- p + geom_histogram(...) # <2>
  } else {
    p <- p + geom_bar(...)
  }

  p  
}
```
1. standard technique for programming with tidy-evaluation: *embracing*.
2. using the ellipsis 

```{r}
#| eval: true
(
  gg_obj(tb, "col_num") +
    labs(
      title= "Histogram", 
      subtitle= "Numerical column")
) +
(
  gg_obj_2(tb, col_num, fill="red") +
    labs(
      title= "Histogram, tuning color", 
      subtitle= "Numerical column")
)
```
 
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

How could you add a geom_point() layer to each element of the following list?

```{r}
plots <- list(
  ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)),
  ggplot(diamonds, aes(carat, price)),
  ggplot(faithfuld, aes(waiting, eruptions, size = density))
)
```

From [R Advanced Programming](https://ggplot2-book.org/programming#exercises-3)

:::


::: {.content-visible when-profile='solution'} 
 
::: {.callout-tip title='Solution'} 
 
```{r}
plots |> 
  map(\(x) x + geom_point()) |>
  patchwork::wrap_plots()
```

## Inside `lm()`    {#sec-inside-lm}

::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

In classes like `lm`, `prcomp`, ... we have a member called `call`. What does it represent? How is it constructed? 

{{< fa hand-point-right >}} First, read the code of `lm`.

:::


```{.r}
> lm 
function (formula, data, subset, weights, na.action, method = "qr", 
    model = TRUE, x = FALSE, y = FALSE, qr = TRUE, singular.ok = TRUE, 
    contrasts = NULL, offset, ...) 
{
    ret.x <- x
    ret.y <- y
    cl <- match.call()    # <1>
    mf <- match.call(expand.dots = FALSE)  # <2>
    m <- match(c("formula", "data", "subset", "weights", "na.action", 
        "offset"), names(mf), 0L)
    mf <- mf[c(1L, m)]
    mf$drop.unused.levels <- TRUE
    mf[[1L]] <- quote(stats::model.frame)
    mf <- eval(mf, parent.frame())   # <3>
    if (method == "model.frame") 
        return(mf)
    else if (method != "qr") 
        warning(gettextf("method = '%s' is not supported. Using 'qr'", 
            method), domain = NA)
    mt <- attr(mf, "terms")
    y <- model.response(mf, "numeric")
    w <- as.vector(model.weights(mf))
    if (!is.null(w) && !is.numeric(w)) 
        stop("'weights' must be a numeric vector")
    offset <- model.offset(mf)
    mlm <- is.matrix(y)
    ny <- if (mlm) 
        nrow(y)
    else length(y)
    if (!is.null(offset)) {
        if (!mlm) 
            offset <- as.vector(offset)
        if (NROW(offset) != ny) 
            stop(gettextf("number of offsets is %d, should equal %d (number of observations)", 
                NROW(offset), ny), domain = NA)
    }
    if (is.empty.model(mt)) {
        x <- NULL
        z <- list(coefficients = if (mlm) matrix(NA_real_, 0, 
            ncol(y)) else numeric(), 
                  residuals = y, 
                  fitted.values = 0 * y, 
                  weights = w, 
                  rank = 0L, 
                  df.residual = if (!is.null(w)) sum(w != 0) else ny
              )
        if (!is.null(offset)) {
            z$fitted.values <- offset
            z$residuals <- y - offset
        }
    }
    else {
        x <- model.matrix(mt, mf, contrasts)
        z <- if (is.null(w)) 
            lm.fit(x, y, offset = offset, singular.ok = singular.ok, 
                ...)
        else lm.wfit(x, y, w, offset = offset, singular.ok = singular.ok, 
            ...)
    }
    class(z) <- c(if (mlm) "mlm", "lm")
    z$na.action <- attr(mf, "na.action")
    z$offset <- offset
    z$contrasts <- attr(x, "contrasts")
    z$xlevels <- .getXlevels(mt, mf)
    z$call <- cl
    z$terms <- mt
    if (model) 
        z$model <- mf
    if (ret.x) 
        z$x <- x
    if (ret.y) 
        z$y <- y
    if (!qr) 
        z$qr <- NULL
    z
}
<bytecode: 0x55564224e930>
<environment: namespace:stats>
```
1. This is where the function stores the calling expressions
2. What is the purpose of optional argument `expand.dots`?
3. What is the purpose of call engineering?

Let us explore the next toy example. 

```{r}
fun <- function(x, lower = 0, upper = 1) {
  structure((x - lower) / (upper - lower), CALL = match.call())
}

type_of(w)

w

str(w)

x <- attr(w, 'CALL')

typeof(x)

is_call(x)

eval(x)  
# try also eval_tidy(), eval_bare
```

## Tidy evaluation   {#sec-tidy-eval}

::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

What is *quasi-quotation*?

Keep the `rlang` cheatsheet around. 

:::

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="solution"}  

```{r}
foo <-  function(df, col, ...){
  cl <- match.call()
  params <- list(...)
  vct <- pull(df, {{col}})
  tp <- class(vct)[1]

  if (tp != "numeric" & tp !="factor") {
    stop("column is of wrong type!")
    return
  }

  p <- ggplot(df) + 
    aes(x={{col}})  # <1>

  if (tp=="numeric") {
    p <- p + geom_histogram(...) # <2>
  } else {
    p <- p + geom_bar(...)
  }

  structure(list(PLOT=p, CALL=cl), class="foobar")  
}
```

```{r}
(
  foo(tb, col_num)$PLOT +
    labs(
      title= "Histogram", 
      subtitle= "Numerical column")
) +
(
  foo(tb, col_num, fill="red")$PLOT +
    labs(
      title= "Histogram, tuning color", 
      subtitle= "Numerical column")
)
```


```{r}
foo(tb, col_num)$PLOT
```




```{r}
foobar <- foo(tb, col_num)$CALL
```



```{r}
rlang::is_expression(foobar)

rlang::eval_bare(foobar)

rlang::eval_tidy(foobar)
```
